Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Minh is a 24-year-old Vietnamese American painter who presented for his initial intake appearing quietly guarded, his eyes moving briefly to the door as he settled into the chair. He had been referred by his primary care physician after a routine visit during which he disclosed, almost incidentally, that he had not been sleeping well for several months. What emerged over the first few sessions was a more complete picture of a young man whose sense of himself and his place in the world had been profoundly disrupted by violence at the hands of someone he had loved.

For nearly two years, Minh had been in a relationship with a partner who became increasingly controlling and, eventually, physically abusive. The abuse escalated gradually, and Minh found himself rationalizing early incidents as anomalies. The episode that brought him to the present crisis occurred approximately eight months ago. He had arrived home late from a mural commission - paint still on his hands - and his partner, who had been waiting, struck him repeatedly in the kitchen of their shared apartment. What Minh remembers most sharply is the sound of a chair scraping against the tile floor just before the first blow, and the particular quality of light in the room - the overhead fixture harsh and humming. Other moments from that evening are simply gone. He cannot reconstruct the sequence with any confidence; there are stretches that feel like film cut from a reel, and then sudden, vivid fragments that arrive without warning and feel, when they come, entirely present-tense. When a memory surfaces, Minh does not experience it as recollection. He experiences it as now.

He ended the relationship shortly afterward and moved into a small studio apartment, but the months since have been marked by a slow contraction of his life. He had come to believe, with a conviction that felt self-evident rather than learned, that the abuse had happened because of something fundamental and defective in him - not because of what his partner did, but because of who Minh was. He described himself as inadequate in a way that felt constitutional, and said more than once that he no longer felt he belonged anywhere in particular - not with his family, not with friends, not in the art community he had once moved through with ease.

At work, Minh paints commercial murals and residential interiors, which requires him to enter unfamiliar buildings regularly. He noted that he now locates the exits of every room within the first moments of entering, a habit so automatic he barely registers doing it until he catches himself doing it in spaces where it makes no practical sense - a client's living room, a coffee shop. When a project runs behind schedule or a client takes longer than expected to respond to a message, he becomes certain that something has gone wrong in a way that is dangerous rather than merely inconvenient. On a recent job, a co-worker's footsteps in an adjacent room caused him to go entirely still, unable to move or speak for several seconds. He has begun turning down evening commissions, telling himself it is a scheduling preference, though the real calculation involves avoiding the specific combination of low light and solitude that tends to bring on disturbed nights.

At home, he keeps the television on at a low volume and finds himself pausing frequently to listen for sounds at the door - the elevator, footsteps in the hallway, anything that might mean someone is approaching. His partner, who moved in with him three months ago and is aware that something is wrong without knowing the full shape of it, has noticed that Minh flinches at unexpected sounds and sometimes seems to look through her rather than at her. He has avoided telling her the details, partly because he does not know how to arrange the memories into a coherent account, and partly because he has come to fear that a full telling would confirm what he already suspects about himself.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a moment in his studio when he found himself unable to finish a painting he had been working on for weeks - standing in front of the canvas, brush in hand, unable to account for a large portion of the previous hour. He came to his first appointment hoping, cautiously, that someone might help him understand what was happening to his mind. What he feared most was that the answer would simply be that this was who he was now.
